newsitem.title: USA: Hooters says ready to resolve harassment suit.
newsitem.headline: Hooters says ready to resolve harassment suit.

text.p: Hooters of America Inc on Tuesday said it was ready to address in arbitration allegations of sexual harassment filed by a former employee.

Hooters has "a longstanding policy of non-harassment and is proud to provide all of its employees a harassment-free work environment," the company said in a statement responding to a lawsuit filed by Annette Phillips, a former waitress and bartender.
The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina, does not seek specific monetary damages.

Phillips worked as a waitress and bartender at Hooters from May 1989 until June 1996, when she left claiming she could no longer bear the working conditions at the restaurant in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina.
A male manager exposed himself to her and a relative of a company executive "slapped and grabbed my rear end," while she was working as a bartender, Phillips said at a news conference on Tuesday.
Attorneys for Phillips said they hoped that publicity about the lawsuit, which came inresponse to a lawsuit filed against Phillips by Hooters, would attract other plaintiffs for a class action.
In its statement, Hooters said it had sued Phillips because of "her refusal to abide by the company's alternative dispute resolution agreement to arbitrate, which she had twice agreed to in writing."

"This suit was not to dissuade her from enforcing her right to a harassment-free work environment," the statement said. "Hooters action protects the rights of thousands of Hooters employees, at all levels, who benefit from this policy."
Hooters, known for its female waitresses and bartenders, who wear very short orange shorts and small white t-shirts, said it was "ready to resolve this dispute."
